source.title: Subspace Fitting Meets Regression: The Effects of Supervision and Orthonormality Constraints on Double Descent of Generalization Errors
source.authors: Yehuda Dar; Paul Mayer; L. Luzi; Richard Baraniuk

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some equations and symbols have extraction artifacts, but the relevant text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests double descent in linear subspace-fitting and regression settings, and finds that its presence depends on supervision and orthonormality constraints; some settings instead show monotone decrease.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test/generalization-error results as parameterization p varies. Cited results from other work are not extracted as rows. Detailed covariance and eigenvalue analyses that do not report a separate test-error outcome are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own out-of-sample error against parameter count p for linear subspace fitting and regression across supervision and orthonormality levels. This bears directly on V4, whether double descent holds beyond deep networks. It shows the curve appears only in supervised, weakly constrained settings and is a single descent elsewhere.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that double descent in linear subspace estimation becomes more evident as problems become more supervised and less orthonormally constrained. Standard unsupervised subspace fitting shows a single descent in p, though overparameterization still lowers error.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic noisy linear data, feature-subset size p as its parameterization axis, and PCA or projected-gradient procedures across supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised settings. It does not reproduce deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve depends on supervision level and orthonormality-constraint strength. For unsupervised feature sweeps, the individual feature-addition order, noise level, and estimated-versus-true subspace dimension also affect monotonicity.

fits_no_version.finding: Orthonormality constraints act like a structural restriction. Tightening them removes interpolation and, with it, the double-descent peak, while overparameterization remains beneficial.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent requires the model class to be able to interpolate. Structural constraints that block interpolation turn the curve into a single descent.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 119, 2020)
record.problems: The experiments use synthetic linear subspace data. Most plotted test-error values are not numerically reported in the text, and the reported experiment averages have no stated error bars or other uncertainty estimates. The authors note that an individual feature-addition order need not have monotone error.
record.rows_left_out: No separate numerical values were extracted from the plots. Appendix A contains additional figure-only curves across subspace constructions, noise levels, dimensions, and feature orders; the text's reported aggregate monotonicity and individual-order caveat are represented in r1-r2.

untested.parts: No deep networks; linear models only.
n is fixed; there is no sample-size sweep.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Noise level and tuned regularization are not varied against the peak; no multiple peaks are examined.

missing.what: Outcomes for each supervision level in the unconstrained semi-supervised sweep. Low-supervision curves (nsup 0-12) appear not to show double descent, while higher levels do.
missing.locator: Section 5, Figure 4a; Appendix C, Figure C.1a

missing.what: Statement that after the peak, errors fall to significantly lower values than in the underparameterized range (supervised, less constrained settings).
Unsupervised fitting with soft orthonormality constraints follows the strict PCA solution for all alpha. The constraint level does not matter without supervision.

record.verdict_notes: I relabelled the record's 'challenges' as limits_scope: V4's claimed benefit past interpolation still appears in the unsupervised settings, only without a peak, and strict constraints never reach interpolation. I dropped the redundant blanket limits_scope label. Results are synthetic and figure-only with no error bars; the first descent is absent by construction.

versions.untested_parts: Changing training sample size near an interpolation threshold.
The study tests linear regression and subspace-fitting settings, not all model classes or a universal curve.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
Whether label noise drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
Recounting complexity using an effective parameter count to determine whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: unsupervised linear subspace fitting (PCA)
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of selected input features p and measure out-of-sample squared error.

conditions.value: errors averaged over 500 uniformly chosen sequential feature orders

rows.value: The error decreases monotonically on average as p increases.
rows.locator: Section 3.4, Figure 2b; Appendix A.5, Figures A.1-A.3
rows.note: The text describes the averaged trend; the plotted numerical values are not stated.
rows.check: State is right: no peak, error averaged over 500 feature orders falls monotonically in p. The second-descent benefit of overparameterization still holds, so this qualifies V4 rather than reversing it.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 3.3–3.4; Figure 2b; Appendix A.5, Figures A.1–A.3.

rows.subject: unsupervised linear subspace fitting (PCA)
rows.operation_detail: Vary p along an individual sequential order of added features and measure out-of-sample squared error.

conditions.value: Hadamard and random constructions; multiple k and noise settings in Appendix A

rows.value: For an individual feature order, monotone decrease is not guaranteed; one plotted curve is explicitly described as non-monotone.
rows.note: The described non-monotonicity is not characterized as a fall-rise-fall curve.
rows.check: A single-order curve is non-monotone because of feature-order noise, not a characterized peak. It cannot show V4's shape.

rows.subject: unsupervised linear subspace fitting (PCA)
rows.size_stated: d=128, n=70; estimated rank k varied
rows.operation_detail: Increase the estimated subspace rank k by extending the learned subspace.
rows.value: The out-of-sample error monotonically decreases as k increases.
rows.note: The paper states a monotone result for this axis.
rows.check: This is a proven proposition (monotone decrease in rank k), not an empirical curve. Locator should include Appendix A.4.

rows.subject: fully supervised subspace fitting with strict orthonormality constraints
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of selected input features p and measure out-of-sample squared error.
rows.value: The error decreases over the range of p; the authors state that this setting has no double-descent behavior.
rows.uncertainty: Errors averaged over 10 experiments with different sequential feature orders; error bars not stated.
rows.note: The corresponding in-sample error does not reach interpolation, even for p>n.
rows.check: Interpolation is never reached under strict constraints, so the interpolation threshold V4 refers to does not occur.

rows.subject: fully supervised unconstrained linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of selected input features p and measure out-of-sample squared error.
rows.value: Double descent is reported; the peak is at p=n−1. The first descent is missing in this construction.
rows.uncertainty: Errors averaged over 10 experiments with different sequential feature orders; error bars not stated.
rows.note: The authors state that the corresponding in-sample error is zero for p≥n−1, due to data centering.

rows.subject: fully supervised subspace fitting with soft orthonormality constraints
rows.operation_detail: Vary p while progressively relaxing the singular-value orthonormality constraint.
rows.value: The trends decrease across p; double descent is absent or only apparent in very weak form.
rows.uncertainty: Errors averaged over 10 experiments with different sequential feature orders; error bars not stated.
rows.note: The paper also says these settings do not achieve accurate interpolation.
rows.check: Authors say the double-descent shape is 'not apparent (or apparent in very weak forms)'. Absent is acceptable; partial for the weak cases. These settings also do not interpolate accurately.

rows.subject: fully supervised subspace fitting with soft orthonormality constraints
rows.operation_detail: Vary p while relaxing the soft orthonormality constraint.
rows.value: Double-descent trends emerge as the orthonormality constraints are relaxed; peaks are at p=n−1, including cases where interpolation begins later.
rows.uncertainty: Errors averaged over 10 experiments with different sequential feature orders; error bars not stated.
rows.note: The paper does not state numerical α values for each plotted curve.

rows.subject: semi-supervised subspace fitting, unconstrained
rows.operation_detail: Vary p across a sweep of supervision levels and measure out-of-sample squared error.
rows.value: The authors report that double descent emerges as supervision increases, including in semi-supervised settings.
rows.uncertainty: Errors averaged over 25 experiments with different sequential feature orders; error bars not stated.
rows.note: The text reports the supervision sweep's trend; it does not separately describe the outcome for each plotted nsup curve.
rows.check: Observed only at higher supervision levels. Low-supervision curves (nsup 0-12, grey dotted) are not described as showing double descent, so the row merges conditions.

relation.reason: Its own theoretical and experimental generalization-error results directly examine double descent in linear subspace fitting and regression.

tranche.reason: The study provides original results showing that the complete double-descent shape depends on supervision and orthonormality constraints, qualifying V4.

source_check.notes: r3 is a general theorem about sequential rank extension, not an experiment restricted to d=128 and n=70. Observed in r8–r9 describes emergence along the sweeps, not double descent in every constituent curve; constrained supervised peaks can precede the interpolation threshold.

statements.correction: Unsupervised PCA: monotone improvement; rank-overparameterized estimates are S-interpolating (Proposition 3.1). Strictly orthonormal supervised fitting: no double descent; interpolation not achieved even for p>n. Both retain benefits from increased parameterization. These results qualify the complete curve.
statements.problem: The study-specific descriptions are accurate when noninterpolation refers to strictly constrained supervised fitting. The challenges label overstates the evidence against V4's improvement beyond interpolation: unsupervised PCA retains improvement, while strictly constrained supervised fitting never reaches interpolation.
